questions.question: In storage structures such as SSTables and B-trees, keeping records sorted by key brings which main benefit and which main cost?

options.text: Lookups and range scans touch only a small region, but writes need extra work to keep the order
Sorted data needs no index of any kind, but every write must then be applied in place on disk
Sorting saves memory, but it weakens durability because sorted files cannot be logged
Sorting removes the need for compaction, but it makes range queries slower than with a hash index

questions.explanation: When records are sorted by key, a lookup only needs to find the neighbourhood of the key: a sparse index can point to a nearby key and the engine scans forward, and a range query reads one contiguous run. The cost is on the write path, because incoming writes arrive in arbitrary order: an LSM engine first sorts them in an in-memory memtable and later merges sorted files, and a B-tree must find the right page and sometimes split it. Sorting does not remove the need for an index, compaction, or a log; it changes what those structures can do cheaply.

questions.question: At the most basic level, what two things must any database do?

options.text: Store data it is given, and return it when asked later
Enforce a declared schema, and answer queries against it
Replicate data across nodes, and tolerate node faults
Index the data for lookup, and compress it for storage

questions.explanation: Every database, whatever its data model, must store data when an application gives it some, and return that data when the application asks for it later. Schemas, replication, fault tolerance, indexing and compression are features that particular databases add to do those two jobs well, but none of them is the basic contract: a schemaless, single-node, unindexed store that can save and return data is still a database.

questions.question: Why should an application developer care how a database handles storage internally, given they will never write a storage engine?

options.text: So you can choose an engine for your workload and reason about tuning it
So you can read and modify the storage engine's source code when needed
So you can implement an equivalent storage engine yourself if needed
Only so you become fluent in the query language the engine exposes

questions.explanation: Storage choices affect which workloads a database handles well, how failures are recovered, and which tuning decisions matter. An application developer needs a working vocabulary and rough mental model, not the expertise required to implement an engine.

questions.question: A shell database appends 'key,value' to a file; a read greps for the key, strips the prefix, and pipes through tail -n 1. Which single element gives 'most recent value' semantics?

options.text: The grep, because it matches only the newest matching line in the file
The tail -n 1: appends never overwrite, so the last match is the newest
The sed, because it discards the stale prefixes as it strips them
The append redirection, because it truncates the prior value first

questions.explanation: Every write appends a new 'key,value' line and never overwrites an older one, so the file can hold several lines for the same key in the order they were written. grep returns every matching line, in file order, not just the newest; sed only removes the 'key,' prefix from each line; and the append redirection adds to the file rather than truncating it. tail -n 1 keeps only the final match, and because lines are appended in time order, the final match is the most recently written value.

questions.question: An append-only shell key-value store writes key 123456 once and key 42 twice. When its data file is printed before compaction, how many lines appear, and why?

options.text: Two lines, one per distinct key, since the second write replaces the first
Three lines, because both writes to key 42 survive the append
Four lines, because each overwrite also appends a tombstone record
One line, because the file is compacted the moment it is read

questions.explanation: Three lines appear: one for key 123456 and two for key 42. Each write appends a new record and never modifies an earlier one, so the first value of key 42 is still in the file. Reads get current-value semantics by taking the last matching record. Tombstones are only written for deletes, not for updates, and nothing compacts the file as a side effect of reading it; compaction is a separate process that later discards superseded records.

questions.question: A toy key-value store writes by appending each 'key,value' line to the end of a file. Why are its writes fast, and what is such a file called in storage-engine terms?

options.text: Appends are cheap sequential writes needing no lookup; the file is a log, an append-only sequence of records
Each write overwrites the old value in place, so the file stays small; the file is a heap file of unordered rows
Writes are first collected in a sorted in-memory tree, so disk writes are batched; the file is a memtable
The whole file stays resident in memory, so writes never touch disk; the file is a write-through cache

questions.explanation: Appending to the end of a file is about the simplest and cheapest write possible: the engine does not need to find or overwrite an older record, and the disk sees sequential writes. A file used this way is a log in the general storage sense: an append-only sequence of records, not necessarily human-readable. Many real databases use a log internally, but they also need to handle concurrency control, reclaiming the space taken by obsolete records, and partially written records after a crash. A memtable is an in-memory sorted tree, and a heap file is updated in place; neither describes this append-only file.

questions.question: The word 'log' is ambiguous. Which sense is meant in storage engines?

options.text: The general sense: an append-only sequence of records, perhaps binary
Application logs: human-readable text describing what is happening in a running program
The write-ahead log, used specifically for crash recovery
The replication stream sent between database nodes

questions.explanation: In storage engines, a log means an append-only sequence of records, often binary and intended only for programs to read. This general meaning recurs in storage, replication, and stream processing, and it is broader than any one use: a write-ahead log and a replication stream are both examples of logs, and application diagnostic logs are just a human-readable special case.

questions.question: A lookup is O(n). With 10,000 records it takes 4 ms. Roughly how long at 10 million records?

options.text: 40 ms
400 ms
4 seconds
40 seconds

questions.explanation: Assume the lookup cost grows linearly with the number of records and the time per record stays constant. Ten million is 1,000 times 10,000, so the lookup takes about 4 ms × 1,000 = 4,000 ms, roughly 4 seconds. That linear growth is why a full scan of the data file for every read does not scale and an index is needed.

questions.question: What is a database index, and why can one be added or dropped without changing what queries return?

options.text: An additional structure derived from the primary data that helps locate records; it affects only query performance, not the data's contents
A compressed copy of the whole table that serves reads instead of the table; dropping it is safe because it is rebuilt on the next read
A cache of recent query results; dropping it is safe because cached entries expire on their own after a timeout
The primary copy of the data kept in sorted order; dropping it is safe because a backup of the table is retained

questions.explanation: An index is extra metadata kept alongside the primary data, acting as a signpost that helps the engine find the records a query wants without scanning everything. Because it is derived from the primary data, adding or removing an index does not change the database's contents; it only changes how fast queries run (and how much work writes do to keep it current). It is not a query-result cache, not a backup, and not the primary copy itself, so dropping it never loses data. Different query patterns may need different indexes on different parts of the data.

questions.question: What is the basic read/write trade-off of adding indexes, and how does it shape which indexes databases create?

options.text: Indexes speed up reads but each slows writes, so the developer or DBA chooses indexes from known query patterns
Indexes speed up writes but slow reads, so databases normally index every column by default to keep writes fast
Indexes cost nothing on SSDs and slow writes only on spinning disks, so modern databases index every column automatically
Indexes cost memory but no extra write work, so databases create as many indexes as available RAM can hold

questions.explanation: An index lets reads locate data quickly, but it is extra structure that must be updated on every write that affects it. Simply appending to a file is the cheapest possible write, and every index adds work on top of that. Because each index slows writes, databases generally do not index everything by default; the developer or administrator picks indexes based on the application's typical queries, aiming for the largest read benefit with the least write overhead. The cost is not specific to spinning disks and is not only a memory cost.

questions.question: A key-value store most closely resembles which familiar programming construct, and why is a key-value index a useful building block?

options.text: A dictionary, usually a hash map; key-value data is common, and more complex indexes build on key-value ones
An array indexed by position; every other index type is implemented internally as an array of fixed-size slots
A singly linked list; records are always traversed in insertion order, which every more complex index relies on
A mathematical set; keys are stored without associated values, which more complex indexes then attach later

questions.explanation: A key-value store maps each key to a value, just like the dictionary type in most programming languages, which is usually implemented as a hash map. Key-value data is extremely common, and key-value indexes are a building block for more complex indexes; for example, a secondary index can be built from a key-value index whose values are lists of row identifiers. The design question then becomes how to turn the familiar in-memory idea into an efficient index for data on disk.

questions.question: Describe the simplest indexing strategy for an append-only log — the write path and the read path.

options.text: An in-memory hash map from each key to its latest byte offset; write: append and update the offset; read: look up and seek
Keep the entire data file in memory; on write, append to it; on read, scan the in-memory copy linearly from start to end
Keep a sorted on-disk index of all keys; on write, re-sort the index file; on read, binary-search the index from scratch
Keep the hash map on disk; on write, rewrite the key's bucket in place; on read, scan the buckets in order until a match

questions.explanation: The simplest index for an append-only data file is an in-memory hash map from each key to the byte offset where that key's value was last written. A write appends the record to the file and sets the key's entry to the new offset, which handles both new keys and updates. A read looks up the offset, seeks to it, and reads the value, without scanning the file. Scanning or re-sorting on each operation, or keeping the hash map on disk, gives up the speed that makes this design attractive.

questions.question: Bitcask (at the time of writing, the default storage engine in Riak) indexes an append-only log with an in-memory hash map from keys to file offsets. What must fit in RAM?

options.text: All keys must fit in RAM; values can exceed memory, since each is read with one disk seek
Both the keys and the values must fit in RAM, because values are served only from the in-memory hash map
Only the values must fit in RAM; the keys can stay on disk because the hash map stores just the values
Neither keys nor values need to fit in RAM, because the hash map itself is paged to disk as it grows

questions.explanation: The hash map holds an entry for every key, mapping it to the byte offset of the key's latest value, and it is kept entirely in memory, so the set of distinct keys must fit in available RAM. Values live in the data file on disk; a read needs only one disk seek to fetch a value, or none if that part of the file is already in the filesystem cache. So the total size of the values can exceed memory, but the number of keys cannot.

questions.question: Bitcask keeps every key in an in-memory hash map pointing at the file offset of the key's latest value. Which workload characteristics make it a good fit? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Each key's value is overwritten very often, e.g. a play counter per video URL incremented on every play
The number of distinct keys is small enough for all keys to fit in RAM, even though the write volume is huge
Reads are mostly point lookups by an exact key rather than scans over key ranges
Queries are predominantly range scans across sorted key ranges

questions.explanation: Bitcask suits workloads with many writes per key but a limited number of distinct keys, such as play counts keyed by video URL. Its hash map has one entry per key, so a huge volume of updates does not make the index bigger, and each read by exact key is one hash lookup plus at most one disk seek. Because a hash table does not keep keys in order, ordered range scans are inefficient and are a poor fit.

optionExplanations.a: Frequent overwrites of the same key are cheap appends in Bitcask, and compaction later discards the many superseded values. A play counter keyed by URL is exactly this update-heavy, small-key-set pattern.
optionExplanations.b: The hash map stores one key-to-offset entry per distinct key, so RAM limits the number of keys, not the number of writes. A small key set can absorb an enormous number of appended updates.
optionExplanations.c: A hash lookup goes straight to the key's latest offset, so exact-key reads cost one lookup and at most one disk seek. That is the access pattern a hash index is designed for.
optionExplanations.d: A hash table does not preserve key order, so a range scan must look up each key individually or scan the log. Sorted structures such as SSTables or B-trees are better suited to range queries.

questions.question: What does compaction do in an append-only key-value log?

options.text: Keeps the newest value for each key and discards superseded entries
Overwrites each old record in place inside the active segment
Deletes the oldest segment even when it holds current values
Truncates every segment whenever the database process restarts

questions.explanation: Compaction throws away duplicate keys in the log, keeping only the most recent value for each key. The writer closes a segment when it reaches a threshold and continues in a new one. Background compaction discards superseded values within segments; merging combines several compacted segments. Because existing segments are immutable, reads can continue while new files are built.

questions.question: In a log-structured store with hash-indexed segment files, why can compaction and merging of segments run without stopping reads and writes? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Segments are never modified after being written, so the merge output is written to a new file
Merging runs in a background thread while old segments still serve requests
When the merge finishes, reads switch to the new file and old ones are deleted
Compaction edits the live segment files in place record by record, so no extra copy is needed

questions.explanation: Closed segments are immutable, so compaction writes a separate merged file while readers continue using the old files and writes go to the current segment. When the merge is complete, the engine switches read requests to the new segment and deletes the obsolete files. Nothing is modified in place, which is what allows the long-running merge to proceed in the background.

optionExplanations.a: Closed segments are immutable, so compaction can read them while writing a completely separate merged segment. Readers never observe a half-rewritten old file.
optionExplanations.b: The background merge does not own the only readable copy; requests continue using the old segments and the current write segment. This separates long merge work from foreground availability.
optionExplanations.c: After the new segment is complete, the engine points reads at it and retires the old files. Switching to a finished file is much safer and shorter than modifying live records throughout the merge.
optionExplanations.d: Editing live segments in place would let readers see half-rewritten records and would break the crash-safety of append-only files. Compaction instead writes a new file and swaps it in when complete.

questions.question: In a log-structured store where each segment file has its own in-memory hash map, how is a key looked up, and what keeps lookups from getting slower and slower?

options.text: Check each segment's hash map, newest first; merging keeps segments few
One global hash map spans every segment, so a single lookup always suffices
All segments are searched in parallel, so their number does not matter
A Bloom filter replaces the per-segment hash maps entirely

questions.explanation: Each segment has its own hash map from keys to offsets. A read checks the most recent segment's map first, because it holds the newest values, then the next older segment, and so on until the key is found. Background merging combines segments and keeps their number small, so a lookup only checks a few hash maps. There is no single global map, searching in parallel does not remove the cost of many segments, and a Bloom filter can only say a key is absent, not give its offset.

questions.question: Which of these are real implementation issues, with the right solution, for a production append-only log with hash indexes such as Bitcask? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: File format — binary with a length prefix beats CSV, and needs no escaping
Deleting records — append a tombstone so merging discards earlier values
Crash recovery — Bitcask snapshots each segment's hash map to speed restart
Checksums on every read path, so a corrupted value is repaired from a replica automatically

questions.explanation: A real hash-indexed log has to deal with several practical issues. A binary format that prefixes each string with its length is faster and simpler than CSV and needs no escaping. Deletes are recorded by appending a tombstone, which tells merging to discard earlier values for that key. After a restart the in-memory hash maps are gone; rebuilding them by reading every segment is slow, so Bitcask stores a snapshot of each segment's hash map on disk. Checksums let the engine detect and ignore partially written or corrupted records, but they do not repair anything from a replica. Writes are usually handled by a single writer thread, while immutable segments can be read concurrently.

optionExplanations.a: A binary record format with explicit lengths can skip directly between fields and represent arbitrary bytes without CSV escaping rules. This makes parsing faster and less ambiguous after a crash.
optionExplanations.b: Deletion must be recorded in an append-only design, so a tombstone marks the key as absent. Later compaction sees the marker and removes both it and older values safely.
optionExplanations.c: Rebuilding every in-memory hash table by scanning large segments can make restart slow. Bitcask stores hint-file snapshots of segment indexes so recovery can reconstruct offsets more quickly.
optionExplanations.d: Checksums detect corrupt records and let the engine ignore damaged portions, but a checksum contains no replacement data. Automatic repair would require a separate replica and repair protocol not supplied by the hash log itself.

questions.question: Instead of overwriting values in place, a key-value store appends every write to a log. What are the arguments in favour of this append-only design? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Appending and merging are sequential writes, much faster than random ones on spinning disks
Crash recovery and concurrency are simpler when segments are immutable
Merging old segments avoids data files getting fragmented over time
Append-only logs never need compaction, since nothing is ever overwritten

questions.explanation: Appending and merging segments are sequential writes, which are much faster than random writes on spinning disks and still somewhat preferable on SSDs. Immutable segments make crash recovery and concurrency simpler: a crash cannot leave a value half old and half new, and readers can share closed segments safely. Merging old segments also prevents data files from becoming fragmented over time. The design does not avoid compaction; it depends on compaction to reclaim the space used by superseded values and tombstones.

optionExplanations.a: Appends and segment merges write large sequential regions, avoiding many random seeks on spinning disks. SSDs reduce the gap, but sequential I/O can still be efficient there.
optionExplanations.b: Immutable records cannot be left half-overwritten by a crash, and readers can safely share closed segments without coordinating in-place mutation. Recovery and concurrency logic therefore become simpler.
optionExplanations.c: Compaction rewrites live values into fresh contiguous segments and discards obsolete files. This periodically removes logical and physical fragmentation instead of letting scattered updates accumulate.
optionExplanations.d: Append-only storage accumulates superseded values and tombstones, so it eventually consumes unbounded space without compaction. “Never overwrite” describes the write path, not freedom from cleanup.

questions.question: What are the main limitations of an in-memory hash index over an append-only log? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The hash table must fit in memory; on-disk hash maps need random I/O and fiddly collision logic
Range queries are inefficient — you must look up every key individually
Hash indexes have no way to represent a deletion, so keys can never be removed
Hash indexes cannot be compacted, so their segment files grow without any bound

questions.explanation: A hash index needs every key in an in-memory hash table, so a very large number of keys will not fit; moving the hash map to disk performs poorly because it needs much random I/O, is expensive to grow, and needs fiddly collision handling. A hash index also does not preserve key order, so a range query such as all keys from kitty00000 to kitty99999 must look up each key individually. Deletion (via tombstones) and compaction work fine with hash-indexed logs, so they are not limitations. Sorted structures such as SSTables remove both real limitations.

optionExplanations.a: The in-memory hash table must contain every key, which bounds the distinct key set by RAM. Moving the table to disk introduces random I/O, collision handling, and expensive growth.
optionExplanations.b: Hashes destroy ordering, so there is no adjacent run for keys between two endpoints. A range query must issue many point lookups or inspect the data another way.
optionExplanations.c: A deletion is representable by appending a tombstone and removing older values during compaction. Lack of deletion support is therefore not a limitation of the design.
optionExplanations.d: Hash-indexed segments can be merged and compacted just like other append-only logs. Compaction is actually what bounds segment growth by removing overwritten and deleted entries.

questions.question: What turns a log-structured segment file into an SSTable (Sorted String Table)?

options.text: Its key-value pairs are sorted by key, and each key appears only once per merged segment file
Each segment is compressed with a block codec and is never modified after it is written
All keys and values have a fixed length, so the file can be binary-searched without an index
Every key in the file is indexed in a complete in-memory hash map of keys to offsets

questions.explanation: An ordinary log segment stores key-value pairs in the order they were written. An SSTable adds the requirement that the pairs are sorted by key, and that each key appears only once in each merged segment, which compaction already ensures. Segments were already immutable before this change, so immutability is not what makes an SSTable. Sorting is what allows a sparse in-memory index instead of a full hash map of every key, and SSTables keep variable-length records rather than relying on fixed-length binary search.

questions.question: Why does merging SSTables work even when the files exceed available memory?

options.text: Like mergesort, it reads the sorted files side by side and copies the lowest key
The files are memory-mapped, so the operating system pages them in and out
Each segment compresses enough to fit in available memory during the merge
Merging reads only the in-memory sparse indexes, never the files themselves

questions.explanation: Each input SSTable is already sorted by key, so the merge works like the merge step of mergesort: read all inputs side by side, look at the first key of each, copy the lowest key to the output, and repeat. Only the current position in each file needs to be in memory, so the files can be far larger than RAM, and the output is again sorted. If the same key appears in several inputs, the value from the most recent segment wins, because each segment holds writes from one period of time. Memory-mapping, compression and in-memory indexes are not what make this possible.

questions.question: An SSTable's sparse in-memory index holds byte offsets for the keys 'handbag' and 'handsome' but not 'handiwork'. How is 'handiwork' looked up?

options.text: Jump to handbag's offset and scan forward until handiwork is found or a larger key is reached
Binary-search the whole segment file from its beginning, using record positions to split the range
Scan the entire segment from the start, since a key missing from the index has no known location
Consult a Bloom filter, which returns the exact byte offset of handiwork inside the segment file

questions.explanation: Because the SSTable is sorted, 'handiwork' can only lie between 'handbag' and 'handsome'. The engine jumps to the offset for 'handbag' and scans forward until it finds 'handiwork' or passes the point where it would be. One index entry every few kilobytes is enough because scanning a few kilobytes is fast. Binary search is hard because records are variable-length, a full scan is unnecessary, and a Bloom filter can only say whether a key might be present, not where it is.

questions.question: In an SSTable whose records are grouped into compressed blocks, what does each entry of the sparse in-memory index point to?

options.text: The start of a compressed block holding several adjacent key-value records
The exact byte offset of every individual record in the segment file
A checksum record that verifies the integrity of the following block
The header of the segment file, from which every block is located

questions.explanation: A sparse index already requires scanning forward from a nearby key, so storing several adjacent records as one compressed block adds little extra work. The index points to the block boundary; decompression then yields the nearby records while saving disk space and I/O bandwidth.

questions.question: In an LSM-style engine that writes sorted SSTable files, how is data sorted by key in the first place when incoming writes arrive in any order?

options.text: Keep the sorted structure in memory — a red-black or AVL tree
Re-sort the file on disk after every write completes
Require clients to submit their writes already in sorted order
Use a hash map on write and sort lazily at read time

questions.explanation: Maintaining a sorted structure on disk is possible, but in memory is much easier, and the tree reads back in sorted order. The in-memory tree is the memtable, and it is what reconciles sorted output with sequential writes.

questions.question: Which statements correctly describe how an LSM-tree engine built from a memtable and SSTables handles writes, reads and cleanup? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: On every write, add the key-value pair to an in-memory balanced tree called the memtable
At a size threshold, flush the memtable as a new immutable SSTable; for reads, check the memtable and then SSTables from newest to oldest
Periodically merge and compact SSTables in the background, discarding overwritten and deleted values
Rewrite the oldest SSTable in place whenever a newer value arrives

questions.explanation: Writes go into an in-memory balanced tree, the memtable, which keeps them sorted. When the memtable exceeds a threshold it is written out as a new immutable SSTable, and reads check the memtable first and then the SSTables from newest to oldest so that later values win. Background merging and compaction combine SSTables and drop overwritten or deleted values. No SSTable is ever rewritten in place; merged output goes to new files that replace old ones when complete.

optionExplanations.a: Writes first enter a balanced in-memory memtable, which maintains key order cheaply while absorbing random updates. A small durability log can protect those not-yet-flushed writes.
optionExplanations.b: Once large enough, the sorted memtable becomes a new immutable SSTable. Reads check the freshest state first—the memtable, then disk segments from newest to oldest—so later values win.
optionExplanations.c: Background compaction merges sorted SSTables and keeps the newest value or deletion for each key. It reduces segment count and reclaims space without mutating the input files.
optionExplanations.d: An SSTable is immutable; a newer value creates another entry in a newer memtable or table. Rewriting the oldest table in place would lose the crash and concurrency advantages of the LSM design.

questions.question: What durability problem remains in a memtable-and-SSTable LSM engine, and how is it fixed?

options.text: A crash loses the memtable; an unsorted on-disk log allows replay
Reads grow slow over time; Bloom filters skip the missing keys
The disk eventually fills up; background compaction reclaims the space
Keys arrive unsorted; a red-black tree restores the ordering

questions.explanation: A crash can destroy writes still present only in the in-memory memtable. The engine therefore appends every write to an on-disk recovery log before acknowledging it. The log need not be sorted because it is replayed only after a crash and discarded once the memtable is flushed.

questions.question: Where do LSM-trees come from, and which systems use them? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: The algorithm is what LevelDB and RocksDB use; LevelDB is a Bitcask alternative in Riak
Cassandra and HBase use similar engines, both inspired by Google's Bigtable paper
Patrick O'Neil et al. named the LSM-tree, building on log-structured filesystems
The LSM-tree was first described in Codd's 1970 paper on the relational model

questions.explanation: The memtable-plus-SSTable algorithm is essentially what LevelDB and RocksDB, embeddable key-value storage libraries, use; LevelDB can be used in Riak instead of Bitcask. Cassandra and HBase use similar engines and were inspired by Google's Bigtable paper, which introduced the terms SSTable and memtable. The structure was originally described by Patrick O'Neil and colleagues as the Log-Structured Merge-Tree, building on log-structured filesystems. Codd's relational model is a logical data model and has nothing to do with this storage algorithm.

optionExplanations.a: LevelDB and RocksDB implement embedded LSM-style key-value storage, and Riak can use LevelDB instead of Bitcask. The products are concrete descendants of the sorted-segment design.
optionExplanations.b: Cassandra and HBase use related storage engines inspired by Google's Bigtable design. Bigtable introduced the SSTable and memtable terminology used for these components.
optionExplanations.c: Patrick O'Neil and coauthors named the log-structured merge-tree, building on ideas from log-structured filesystems. The lineage explains the append-and-merge rather than overwrite-in-place approach.
optionExplanations.d: Codd's 1970 work introduced the relational data model, not the LSM-tree storage algorithm. Relational abstraction and physical index implementation are separate layers.

questions.question: How does Lucene reuse the SSTable idea?

options.text: Its term dictionary maps a word to a postings list in sorted files
It stores documents as SSTables while keeping its terms in a B-tree
It uses SSTables purely to cache the results of previous queries
It uses in-memory hash indexes rather than any sorted structure

questions.explanation: Lucene, the full-text indexing engine behind Elasticsearch and Solr, keeps a term dictionary: a key-value structure whose key is a word (term) and whose value is the postings list, the IDs of all documents containing that word. That mapping is stored in sorted, SSTable-like files that are merged in the background, the same idea as an LSM-tree. It is not a query-result cache, does not use a B-tree for terms, and does rely on sorted structures rather than hash indexes.

questions.question: Which kind of lookup is slow in an LSM-tree, and what common optimization addresses it?

options.text: Absent-key lookups, which check every segment; Bloom filters rule them out
Range scans, which sparse in-memory indexes are added to accelerate
Sequential writes, which the write-ahead log absorbs on the engine's behalf
Point lookups of keys that do exist, which compaction makes faster

questions.explanation: To conclude that a key does not exist, an LSM-tree must check the memtable and then every SSTable back to the oldest, possibly reading disk for each one. A Bloom filter is a memory-efficient structure that approximates the contents of a set: it can say a key is definitely absent (it may give false positives, but never false negatives), so the engine can skip SSTables that cannot contain the key. Range scans are already efficient because the data is sorted, and sequential writes are an LSM strength, not a weakness.

questions.question: In LSM-tree storage engines, how does leveled compaction differ from size-tiered compaction?

options.text: Size-tiered merges newer, smaller SSTables into older, larger ones; leveled splits the key range into smaller SSTables arranged in levels, compacting more incrementally
Leveled merges newer, smaller SSTables into older, larger ones; size-tiered splits the key range into smaller SSTables arranged in levels, compacting more incrementally
Size-tiered removes only tombstones from SSTables, whereas leveled removes only overwritten values and leaves tombstones in place
Size-tiered rewrites each SSTable in place on disk, whereas leveled appends every new value to a single ever-growing SSTable

questions.explanation: Both strategies decide the order and timing of SSTable merges. In size-tiered compaction, newer and smaller SSTables are successively merged into older and larger ones. In leveled compaction, the key range is split into smaller SSTables and older data is moved into separate levels, which lets compaction proceed more incrementally and use less disk space. At the time of writing, LevelDB (hence its name) and RocksDB used leveled compaction, HBase used size-tiered, and Cassandra supported both. Both strategies drop overwritten values and tombstones, and neither modifies SSTables in place.

questions.question: What is the basic idea of an LSM-tree, and what does it deliver?

options.text: Sorted SSTables merged in the background; scales past memory, serves range queries, and sustains high write throughput
A single B-tree kept in memory and flushed periodically; faster for reads than for writes, because pages stay sorted on disk
An in-memory hash map over an append-only log; needs every key to fit in memory, and cannot serve range queries efficiently
A set of unsorted log segments merged only on demand; gives high write throughput, but cannot support range queries at all

questions.explanation: An LSM-tree keeps a cascade of SSTables, sorted files that are merged and compacted in the background. Because only the memtable must be in memory, it keeps working when the dataset is much larger than RAM. Because the data is sorted, range queries are efficient, and because disk writes are sequential, it supports very high write throughput. The hash-map-over-log design needs all keys in memory and cannot scan ranges, which is exactly what sorted SSTables fix.

questions.question: As of the late 2010s, how did B-trees compare with log-structured indexes in how widely they were used?

options.text: B-trees were the most widely used index, standard in almost all relational databases; log-structured indexes were gaining acceptance
Log-structured indexes had replaced B-trees as the standard index in almost all relational databases, and B-trees survived mainly in older systems
B-trees were used only in relational databases, while every nonrelational database used log-structured indexes exclusively
B-trees were a recent design that had not yet been adopted outside research systems, while log-structured indexes were ubiquitous

questions.explanation: B-trees were introduced in 1970 and were already called ubiquitous less than ten years later. They remain the standard index implementation in almost all relational databases, and many nonrelational databases use them too. Log-structured indexes were gaining acceptance and were increasingly popular in new datastores, but they were not the most common type of index.

questions.question: B-trees and SSTable-based log-structured indexes both keep key-value pairs sorted by key. How do they differ in the unit of storage they read and write?

options.text: Log-structured indexes write variable-size segments of several megabytes sequentially; B-trees read and write fixed-size pages, traditionally 4 KB, one at a time
B-trees write variable-size segments of several megabytes sequentially; log-structured indexes read and write fixed-size pages, traditionally 4 KB, one at a time
Both use fixed-size 4 KB pages, but B-trees always append new pages while log-structured indexes overwrite them in place
Both write variable-size segments, but B-trees overwrite whole segments in place while log-structured indexes append them

questions.explanation: Log-structured indexes break the database into variable-size segments, typically several megabytes or more, and always write a segment sequentially. B-trees break the database into fixed-size pages, traditionally 4 KB, and read or write one page at a time, which matches the fixed-size blocks of the underlying disk. Pages have addresses, so one page can refer to another, which is how a B-tree builds its tree of pages. This difference in write unit underlies most of the later performance trade-offs.

questions.question: In a B-tree, what is the branching factor, and why is a large branching factor useful?

options.text: The number of child-page references in an internal page; often several hundred, keeping the tree shallow
The number of levels from the root to a leaf page; usually three or four, which bounds the cost of a lookup
The number of keys stored in each leaf page; often several thousand, which reduces how often pages split
The ratio of internal pages to leaf pages; usually about ten, which keeps the tree balanced after inserts

questions.explanation: In a B-tree, each internal page holds keys that act as boundaries plus references to child pages, and each child covers one sub-range of keys. The branching factor is the number of child-page references in one such page. The more references a page holds, the more sub-ranges each level splits the key range into, so the tree needs fewer levels to cover all keys, and a lookup reads fewer pages from root to leaf. The value depends on the page size and on how much space the boundary keys and page references take; in practice it is typically several hundred. The depth (often three or four levels) is a consequence of the branching factor, not the branching factor itself.

questions.question: In a B-tree, what happens when you update the value of an existing key, and what happens when you insert a new key?

options.text: An update rewrites the key's leaf page in place; an insert adds the key to its page, splitting it if full
Both append a new version of the key to the end of a file and leave the old page untouched until compaction
An update splits the key's page into two half-full pages, whereas an insert simply overwrites an existing page
Both rewrite the root page to record a new version of the tree, without touching the leaf pages

questions.explanation: To update an existing key, a B-tree finds the leaf page containing it, changes the value in that page, and writes the page back; references to the page stay valid. To insert a new key, it finds the page whose range covers the key and adds it there. If the page has no free space, it is split into two half-full pages and the parent page is updated to reflect the new division of key ranges. Appending new versions and compacting later describes log-structured engines, not B-trees.

questions.question: A four-level B-tree of 4 KB pages with a branching factor of 500 can store up to roughly how much data, and how deep are most databases' B-trees?

options.text: 256 TB, and most databases are three or four levels deep
256 GB, with a typical depth of six or seven levels
2.56 PB, with a typical depth of only two levels
25.6 TB, with a typical depth of about ten levels

questions.explanation: With a branching factor of 500, four levels give 500 × 500 × 500 × 500 = 62,500,000,000 leaf pages. Taking 4 KB as 4,096 bytes, that is about 2.56 × 10^14 bytes, roughly 256 TB (assuming every page is full). Because a B-tree stays balanced, its depth grows only logarithmically with the number of keys, so most databases fit in a tree three or four levels deep and a lookup follows only a few page references.

questions.question: What is the basic write operation of a standard B-tree, and what does it assume?

options.text: Overwrite a page on disk with new data, assuming its location does not change so all references to it stay valid
Append the changed key-value pair to the end of a segment file, assuming older copies are removed later by compaction
Insert the change into an in-memory sorted tree, assuming it will be flushed to a new sorted file when the tree is full
Buffer every change in memory until commit, assuming the operating system writes the pages out in key order

questions.explanation: A B-tree's basic write overwrites a page on disk in place, and it assumes the page stays at the same location, so every reference to that page from its parent remains correct. That is the opposite of log-structured indexes, which only append to files and never modify them in place. On a magnetic disk this means moving the head and overwriting a sector; on an SSD it is more complicated because large blocks must be erased and rewritten. Some B-tree variants (such as LMDB's copy-on-write) write modified pages to new locations instead, but that is an optimization, not the basic operation.

questions.question: In a B-tree, why can a single insert require several page overwrites, and what structure protects against a crash partway through?

options.text: Because a split rewrites both halves and the parent; a write-ahead log guards it
Because pages are compressed on write; per-page checksums detect the damage
Because every insert also rewrites the root page; a read cache keeps a clean copy of it
Because leaves are chained together; sibling pointers repair the chain

questions.explanation: If an insert overfills a page, the page is split: both resulting pages must be written and the parent page must be overwritten to reference them. If the database crashes after only some of those writes, the index can be corrupted, for example with an orphan page that has no parent. B-trees therefore usually keep a write-ahead log (WAL, also called a redo log), an append-only file to which every modification is written before it is applied to the tree pages; after a crash the log is used to restore the tree to a consistent state.

questions.question: In a log-structured storage engine, why do immutable segment files simplify concurrent reads during compaction?

options.text: New segments can be built privately and then published atomically
Every segment update is protected by distributed consensus
All log-structured engines stop readers while a merge is running
Immutable segments remove the need to coordinate metadata changes

questions.explanation: Because existing segments are never modified, compaction can build new merged files privately while queries keep reading the old ones, and then switch to the new files atomically. A B-tree that updates pages in place must instead protect its structures with latches (lightweight locks) so that a reader never sees a half-finished change. Immutability does not remove the need to coordinate the switch itself, does not require distributed consensus, and does not require stopping readers.

questions.question: Which optimizations do real B-tree implementations use? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Copy-on-write — write the modified page elsewhere and create new parent versions (LMDB)
Abbreviated keys — interior pages need only boundaries, so more keys fit per page
Sequential leaf layout and sibling pointers, to scan in order without revisiting parents
Bloom filters on every interior page, so a lookup can skip levels that cannot hold the key

questions.explanation: Common optimizations include copy-on-write pages instead of a write-ahead log, abbreviated keys in interior pages, attempts to keep neighboring leaves physically close, extra sibling pointers, and fractal-tree variants that buffer updates. Bloom filters instead address unnecessary SSTable reads in LSM-based engines.

optionExplanations.a: Copy-on-write writes a changed page elsewhere and builds new parent paths, so the old tree remains a consistent snapshot until publication. LMDB uses this alternative to overwriting pages under a WAL.
optionExplanations.b: Interior pages only need separator boundaries, not complete leaf keys, so abbreviated keys increase the branching factor. More child references per page reduce tree depth.
optionExplanations.c: Keeping neighboring leaves physically close improves ordered scans, and sibling links let traversal continue without returning through parent pages. Growth can make physical adjacency harder to maintain.
optionExplanations.d: Bloom filters answer whether a key is definitely absent from an SSTable and are associated with LSM read optimization. Skipping arbitrary B-tree levels would break the parent-child search path.

questions.question: In a B-tree, how does abbreviating the keys stored in interior pages lead to fewer disk reads per lookup?

options.text: More keys per page, a higher branching factor, fewer levels, fewer page reads
Shorter keys compress better, so each page is smaller and loads from disk faster
Shorter keys shorten how long each page latch is held, so fewer reads must wait
Shorter keys leave room to inline the sibling pointers in each page

questions.explanation: Interior pages only need keys that mark the boundaries between child key ranges, so those keys can be shortened. Since pages have a fixed size, shorter keys let each page hold more keys and child references, which raises the branching factor. A higher branching factor means fewer levels are needed to cover all the keys, and because a lookup reads one page per level, fewer levels means fewer page reads. Compression, latch hold time and sibling pointers are separate concerns.

questions.question: Consider three claims: (1) a B-tree page moves to a new location every time it is overwritten; (2) a B-tree's write-ahead log is written after the tree pages are updated; (3) fractal trees, a B-tree variant, are named for their self-similar geometry. Which assessment is right?

options.text: All three are false
All three are true
Only the first is false
Only the third is false

questions.explanation: A B-tree overwrite normally preserves the page's location so existing references remain valid. The write-ahead log must be durable before the page change so recovery can redo it after a crash. “Fractal tree” is a product term for buffered update techniques, not a claim about geometric self-similarity.

questions.question: As a rule of thumb, how do LSM-trees and B-trees compare on reads and writes, and how firm is that rule?

options.text: LSM-trees are usually faster for writes, B-trees for reads, but benchmarks are often inconclusive
LSM-trees are faster for both reads and writes in essentially every benchmark, so the comparison is settled
B-trees are faster for writes and LSM-trees are faster for reads, consistently across workloads
B-trees are faster for both reads and writes, because their implementations are more mature

questions.explanation: LSM-trees are typically faster for writes because they write sorted files sequentially. B-trees are thought to be faster for reads because an LSM-tree read may need to check several data structures and SSTables at different stages of compaction. This is only a rule of thumb: benchmarks are often inconclusive and sensitive to workload details, so you need to test with your own workload. B-tree maturity is a real difference but does not make them faster at everything.

questions.question: What is write amplification, and at minimum how many times does a B-tree with a write-ahead log write each piece of data?

options.text: One database write causing multiple disk writes over time; a B-tree writes data at least twice
The ratio of an index's size to the data's size; a B-tree writes each piece of data exactly once
The growth of the log file over time; a B-tree writes each piece of data at least three times
The number of pages a query reads; a B-tree writes each piece of data at least four times

questions.explanation: Write amplification is the effect where one write to the database results in multiple writes to disk over the database's lifetime. A B-tree writes every piece of data at least twice: once to the write-ahead log and once to the tree page, and possibly again when pages split. It also writes whole pages even if only a few bytes changed. Log-structured indexes amplify writes too, because compaction and merging rewrite data several times. Index size and pages read per query are different metrics.

questions.question: Which costs does write amplification impose on a storage engine? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Hardware wear, since SSD blocks tolerate only a limited number of overwrites
Throughput, since more disk writes mean fewer writes per second within the bandwidth
Increased read latency caused by growing file fragmentation
Higher memory consumption for the engine's write buffer

questions.explanation: Write amplification means each logical write turns into several physical writes. That matters for the device: SSDs can overwrite blocks only a limited number of times before wearing out. It also matters for throughput: in a write-heavy application where disk write bandwidth is the bottleneck, the more a storage engine writes to disk, the fewer database writes per second it can handle. Fragmentation and write-buffer memory are separate issues, not consequences of write amplification.

optionExplanations.a: Every extra physical rewrite consumes some of an SSD flash block's limited number of program/erase cycles. Write amplification therefore increases device wear beyond the application's logical write volume.
optionExplanations.b: Disk bandwidth spent rewriting the same logical data cannot be used for new incoming writes. When disk writes are the bottleneck, amplification directly lowers the sustainable writes per second.
optionExplanations.c: Fragmentation can affect reads and space usage, but it comes from page splits and partly filled pages, not from writing the same data several times. It is a different problem from write amplification.
optionExplanations.d: A larger write buffer uses memory but is a configuration choice, not a consequence of extra physical writes. Write amplification is about how many bytes reach the disk per logical write.

questions.question: Why are LSM-trees typically able to sustain higher write throughput than B-trees?

options.text: They sometimes have lower write amplification and write compact SSTables sequentially instead of overwriting pages
They update B-tree-like pages in place but batch the changes, so fewer scattered pages are rewritten on each write
They acknowledge writes before anything durable reaches the disk, so disk speed does not limit how fast writes complete
They defer background merging to idle periods, so compaction does not compete with incoming writes for disk bandwidth

questions.explanation: LSM engines may have lower write amplification for some configurations and workloads, though that is not universal, and they write compact SSTable files sequentially rather than overwriting several scattered pages of a tree. Sequential writes are especially advantageous on magnetic hard drives, where they are much faster than random writes; SSD firmware reduces the difference but does not remove it. LSM engines do not overwrite pages in place, still keep a durable log for the memtable before acknowledging writes, and still spend bandwidth on compaction that competes with incoming writes.

questions.question: Why can an LSM-tree use less storage than a B-tree?

options.text: Splits leave B-tree pages partly empty, while compaction rewrites LSM data into dense, well-compressed SSTables
An LSM-tree stores each key in a single place, whereas a B-tree keeps a full copy of each key at every level of the tree
An LSM-tree omits the write-ahead log, whereas a B-tree must keep its log entries on disk until the next backup
An LSM-tree indexes its files with a hash map, which takes much less disk space than the sorted pages of a B-tree

questions.explanation: B-tree storage leaves some disk space unused through fragmentation: when a page splits, or a row cannot fit into an existing page, part of a fixed-size page stays empty. LSM-trees are not page-oriented and periodically rewrite SSTables during compaction, removing fragmentation and producing dense files that compress well, especially with leveled compaction. It is B-trees, not LSM-trees, that store each key in one place; both designs use a log; and LSM-trees index sorted files rather than using a hash map.

questions.question: What is a main downside of LSM-tree compaction for query response times, and where does it show up most?

options.text: Compaction competes with live requests for disk resources, so high-percentile response times can be high
Compaction can silently corrupt records, so every read must verify a checksum and retry, which slows all queries
Compaction requires taking the database offline periodically, so queries fail entirely during each merge
Compaction raises average response time sharply, while leaving the high-percentile response times unaffected

questions.explanation: Disks have limited resources, so even incremental compaction can make a request wait while the disk finishes an expensive merge. The effect on throughput and average response time is usually small, but at high percentiles the response times of log-structured engines can sometimes be quite high, whereas B-trees can be more predictable. Compaction does not require taking the database offline and does not corrupt data; the problem is tail latency, so it shows up in high percentiles rather than averages.

questions.question: In an LSM-tree under high write throughput, what happens if compaction is not configured carefully and cannot keep up with incoming writes?

options.text: Unmerged SSTables pile up, reads slow down because they must check more files, and the disk can eventually run out of space
Read latency is unaffected, since a lookup only ever checks the newest SSTable for each key
Compaction pauses all incoming writes while it runs, so writes stall briefly but the number of segments on disk stays constant
The memtable grows without limit in memory because flushing stops, while the disk usage of SSTables stays flat

questions.explanation: Disk write bandwidth is shared between the initial writes (logging and flushing memtables) and background compaction, and compaction needs more bandwidth as the database grows. If compaction falls behind, the number of unmerged segments keeps growing until the disk fills, and reads slow down because they check more files. Unmerged SSTables are not free: each one is another file a read may have to check, and superseded values keep using disk space. At the time of writing, SSTable-based engines typically did not throttle incoming writes in this situation (some, such as RocksDB, can stall writes when too many files accumulate), so operators need explicit monitoring to detect it.

questions.question: Why are B-trees attractive for databases that want to offer strong transactional semantics?

options.text: Each key exists in exactly one place in the index, so locks on key ranges can be attached directly to the tree
B-trees need no write-ahead log, because each page overwrite is atomic and cannot be interrupted by a crash
B-trees compress better than SSTables, so the locks taken on their pages occupy less memory and disk space
B-trees are the only index structure that supports range queries, which every transaction needs to run

questions.explanation: In a B-tree each key exists in exactly one place, whereas a log-structured engine may hold several copies of the same key in different segments. Many relational databases implement transaction isolation using locks on ranges of keys, and in a B-tree those locks can be attached directly to the tree. B-trees do need a write-ahead log, generally compress worse than LSM-trees, and are not the only structure that supports range queries.

questions.question: Comparing B-trees and LSM-trees overall, which judgment is most defensible?

options.text: B-trees are ingrained and consistently good, log-structured indexes are rising in new datastores, so test empirically
LSM-trees have overtaken B-trees in new and existing systems, so B-trees are mainly kept for compatibility
B-trees are faster on mixed read/write workloads, so log-structured indexes fit mainly write-heavy niche systems
A simple rule settles it, so no testing is needed: use LSM-trees for write-heavy loads and B-trees for read-heavy ones

questions.explanation: B-trees are ingrained in database architecture and give consistently good performance for many workloads, so they are unlikely to go away. Log-structured indexes are becoming increasingly popular in new datastores. Because benchmarks are sensitive to workload details, there is no quick and easy rule for which is better; the choice should be tested empirically with your own workload.

questions.question: A key-value index is like a primary-key index. What does a primary key uniquely identify in a relational, a document, and a graph database respectively?

options.text: A row, a document, and a vertex
A column, a field, and an edge
A page, a collection, and a subgraph
A table, a database, and a whole graph

questions.explanation: In each model, a unique identifier resolves one top-level entity: a row in a relational table, a document in a document database, or a vertex in a graph. Other records can store that identifier as a reference.

questions.question: How are secondary indexes created in relational databases, and why are they crucial?

options.text: With CREATE INDEX; they are crucial for performing joins efficiently
Automatically by the optimizer; they are crucial for durability
With ALTER TABLE; they are crucial for enforcing uniqueness
With CREATE VIEW; they are crucial for hiding columns from users

questions.explanation: A relational database normally creates a secondary index with CREATE INDEX on a non-primary-key column. Such indexes are crucial for joins because they let the engine find all rows carrying a referenced key without scanning the entire table.

questions.question: A secondary index can easily be constructed from a key-value index. What is the main difference, and what are the two ways to solve it?

options.text: Keys aren't unique; list row IDs per key, or append a row ID to each key
They cannot be sorted; solved by hashing or by partitioning the index
They cannot be updated; solved by rebuilding or by versioning entries
They must be clustered; solved by covering columns or by interleaving

questions.explanation: Unlike a primary key, a secondary-index value may match many rows. The index can therefore map one value to a postings list of row IDs, or make each entry unique by combining the indexed value with a row identifier. Either representation can be implemented with B-trees or log-structured storage.

questions.question: Define a heap file and describe what happens when an updated value grows too large to overwrite in place.

options.text: A file of rows in no particular order that indexes point to; an outgrown row moves, and indexes are updated or a forwarding pointer left
A file kept sorted by primary key that indexes point to; a value that grows too large is compressed until it fits back into its original page
An in-memory structure holding the most frequently read rows; a value that grows too large is spilled to disk and dropped from memory
The write-ahead log itself, read by every index; a value that grows too large is split across several consecutive B-tree leaf pages

questions.explanation: An index's value can be the row itself or a reference to a row stored elsewhere. In the latter case rows live in a heap file, which keeps them in no particular order (it may be append-only or reuse space from deleted rows). This avoids duplicating data when there are several secondary indexes, because each index just references a heap location. A value that grows can be overwritten in place only if it still fits; otherwise it is moved to a new heap location, and either every index is updated to the new location or a forwarding pointer is left in the old one.

questions.question: What defines a clustered index?

options.text: The indexed rows themselves are stored within the index, instead of in a separate heap file
The index stores only pointers to rows in a heap file kept in insertion order
The index stores a few selected columns of each row next to the key, the same as a covering index
The index groups rows by a partition key so that each machine holds one group

questions.explanation: A clustered index stores the indexed row data directly within the index, which avoids the extra hop from an index entry to a heap file on reads. For example, in MySQL's InnoDB the primary key is always a clustered index and secondary indexes refer to the primary key; SQL Server lets you specify one clustered index per table. A nonclustered index stores only references, and a covering index is a compromise that stores some of the columns.

questions.question: Between a clustered index (all row data stored in the index) and a nonclustered index (only references stored), what is the compromise, and what is said when it alone can answer a query?

options.text: A covering index, storing some columns; it is said to cover the query
A partial index, storing some rows; it is said to satisfy the query
A concatenated index, combining columns; it is said to span the query
A sparse index, storing some keys; it is said to short-circuit the query

questions.explanation: A covering index, also called an index with included columns, stores some of a table's columns inside the index. If a query needs only those columns, it can be answered from the index alone, without going to the heap file or clustered index; the index is then said to cover the query. Partial, concatenated and sparse indexes are different ideas: they restrict rows, combine key columns, or index only some keys.

questions.question: Clustered and covering indexes speed up reads. At what cost? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They require additional storage space
They can add overhead on writes
The database must work harder so duplication never shows as inconsistency
They make range queries unusable on the indexed columns

questions.explanation: Clustered and covering indexes duplicate or reorganize data to avoid extra reads. That consumes storage, increases write work, and requires transactional maintenance so the duplicated representation never becomes inconsistent with the base row.

optionExplanations.a: Covering and clustered layouts store extra values in or alongside an index, or reorganize the base rows into index order. Those duplicated representations consume additional space.
optionExplanations.b: Every insert or update may need to maintain the clustered layout and copied covering fields. Faster reads are purchased with more write work.
optionExplanations.c: The index copy and base record must change atomically so readers never see contradictory values. Transactional maintenance is necessary precisely because duplication creates inconsistency risk.
optionExplanations.d: Clustering rows by an indexed order can make range scans faster, not unusable, because nearby keys are stored together. The trade-offs are storage and write maintenance rather than loss of ordered querying.

questions.question: A concatenated index on (lastname, firstname), like a paper phone book, can efficiently answer which queries?

options.text: Everyone with a given last name, or last-name/first-name pair, but not everyone with a given first name
All people with a given last name, a given first name, or a given full name, all equally efficiently
Only exact matches on the full (lastname, firstname) pair, because the combined key is hashed
All people with a given first name, but not all people with a given last name, since the last column sorts first

questions.explanation: A concatenated index combines several fields into one key by appending one column to another in a defined order, here last name then first name. Entries are sorted by last name first and by first name only within the same last name. So the index can find everyone with a given last name, or a specific last-name/first-name combination, but people with the same first name are scattered throughout, making the index useless for a first-name-only search. The key is sorted, not hashed, which is why prefix lookups work.

questions.question: A restaurant search filters latitude within a narrow band AND longitude within a narrow band. Why can't a standard B-tree or LSM-tree answer it efficiently?

options.text: It orders entries by one key, so it can narrow only one of the two ranges
Because floating-point coordinates cannot be stored as index keys at all
Because the predicates are combined with AND rather than OR
Because latitude and longitude live in separate tables

questions.explanation: A standard B-tree or LSM-tree index orders entries along one key. An index on latitude can return all restaurants in the latitude band but at any longitude, and an index on longitude returns the longitude band anywhere between the poles; neither can narrow both ranges at once. Floating-point values can be indexed, AND is not the problem, and both columns live in the same table. Answering such a two-dimensional range query efficiently needs a multi-dimensional index.

questions.question: What are common ways to index two-dimensional data such as restaurant latitude and longitude so that map-rectangle queries are efficient?

options.text: Map the location to one number via a space-filling curve and use a B-tree, or more commonly use a spatial index like an R-tree
Build one B-tree per dimension and intersect their results, which is all that specialized spatial indexes such as R-trees do internally
Hash each latitude/longitude pair into a hash index, which supports range queries over map rectangles directly
Use a concatenated index on (latitude, longitude), which restricts both coordinate ranges efficiently in one scan

questions.explanation: One option is to translate a two-dimensional location into a single number using a space-filling curve and then index that number in a regular B-tree. More commonly, specialized spatial indexes such as R-trees are used; for example, PostGIS implements geospatial indexes as R-trees using PostgreSQL's Generalized Search Tree (GiST) facility. Separate one-dimensional indexes or a concatenated index can narrow only one range efficiently, and a hash index does not support range queries at all.

questions.question: Which statements about non-geographic multi-dimensional indexes are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Weather data can use a two-dimensional (date, temperature) index to constrain both ranges
Ecommerce can use a three-dimensional (red, green, blue) index to search a colour range
A one-dimensional date index can also constrain any temperature range without filtering
HyperDex is limited to geospatial latitude-and-longitude indexing

questions.explanation: Multi-dimensional indexes are useful beyond geography. A weather index on date and temperature can constrain both ranges together, and an RGB index can search a region of colour space. A date-only index must still filter temperatures after fetching the date range. HyperDex applies multi-dimensional indexing to database attributes rather than being limited to maps.

optionExplanations.a: A two-dimensional index treats date and temperature as coordinates, so a query for one year's observations within a temperature band selects that rectangle directly. A date-only index would retrieve the whole year before filtering on temperature.
optionExplanations.b: Red, green, and blue values form a three-dimensional colour space, so a colour range can be searched as one region rather than as three unrelated one-dimensional ranges. This is a genuine non-geographic use of the same indexing idea.
optionExplanations.c: A one-dimensional date index orders only by date and cannot simultaneously narrow an arbitrary temperature interval. The engine must inspect the selected date rows and discard temperatures outside the requested range.
optionExplanations.d: HyperDex used multi-dimensional indexing over general database attributes, such as date and temperature, not only map coordinates. Calling it geospatial-only misses the point that the technique applies to any set of dimensions.

questions.question: Standard hash, B-tree and LSM-tree indexes assume what about the keys being queried, and what do full-text search engines add?

options.text: They assume exact keys or ranges; search engines add synonyms, word variants, proximity and edit-distance matching
They assume the data is already sorted; search engines add compression of the index itself so it fits in memory
They assume every key is unique; search engines relax this to allow duplicate keys in a single index
They assume numeric keys throughout; search engines extend the same structures to string keys

questions.explanation: These indexes let you query an exact key, or a range of keys in sort order, but not search for similar keys such as misspelled words. Full-text search engines add fuzzy features: expanding a word to synonyms, ignoring grammatical variations, finding words near each other in a document, and, in Lucene, finding words within a given edit distance (an edit distance of 1 means one letter added, removed, or replaced). Such fuzzy querying needs different techniques from exact-match indexes. Ordinary indexes already handle string keys and non-unique keys.

questions.question: What transformation lets Lucene perform fuzzy term lookup efficiently?

options.text: A finite-state term dictionary becomes a Levenshtein automaton
A sparse SSTable offset map becomes a relational hash join
The postings lists are converted into Bloom filters that tolerate typos
A Bloom filter becomes an edit-distance lookup table

questions.explanation: Lucene stores its term dictionary in a compact trie-like finite-state representation and transforms it into a Levenshtein automaton that accepts terms within a chosen edit distance. LevelDB's in-memory index has a simpler job: it sparsely points into sorted SSTable blocks.

questions.question: Disks need data laid out carefully for good performance. Which advantages make databases tolerate them anyway, and which of those advantages is weakening as RAM gets cheaper?

options.text: Disks are durable and cheaper per gigabyte than RAM; the cost advantage is eroding
Disks are durable and faster than RAM for random reads; the speed advantage is eroding
Disks are cheaper per gigabyte and need no layout tuning; the tuning advantage is eroding
Disks are cheaper per gigabyte and durable; durability is eroding as disks become less reliable

questions.explanation: Both magnetic disks and SSDs are awkward compared with main memory, because data must be laid out carefully for good read and write performance. They are tolerated for two reasons: they are durable (contents survive a power loss) and they cost less per gigabyte than RAM. As RAM gets cheaper, the cost argument weakens, and many datasets are small enough to keep entirely in memory, possibly across several machines, which led to in-memory databases. Disks were never faster than RAM, and durability is not what is eroding.

questions.question: Which statements about in-memory data stores and durability are correct? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Memcached is for caching only, where losing data on restart is acceptable
Durability can come from special hardware such as battery-powered RAM, or from writing a log of changes to disk
Durability can also come from writing periodic snapshots to disk, or from replicating the in-memory state to other machines
An in-memory database forfeits durability by definition, which is why Memcached is typical

questions.explanation: Some in-memory stores, such as Memcached, are meant only for caching, where losing data on restart is acceptable. Others aim for durability using special hardware such as battery-powered RAM, a log of changes written to disk, periodic snapshots written to disk, or replication of the in-memory state to other machines. After a restart such a database reloads its state from disk or from a replica, unless special hardware preserved it. Being in-memory describes where the data is served from, not an absence of durability.

optionExplanations.a: Memcached is a disposable cache: the authoritative data exists elsewhere, so losing memory on restart is acceptable. That makes persistence overhead unnecessary for its intended role.
optionExplanations.b: Battery-backed RAM can preserve memory through power loss, while an append-only disk log records changes for replay. Either mechanism adds durability without moving the normal read path out of RAM.
optionExplanations.c: Periodic snapshots bound restart work, and replication lets a restarted node copy state from another machine. These mechanisms protect or reconstruct volatile working state.
optionExplanations.d: “In-memory” describes where the active data structures and query path live, not an absolute ban on logs, snapshots, or replicas. Durable in-memory databases are therefore possible.

questions.question: An in-memory database may write to disk. Why is it still called in-memory?

options.text: Normal reads and updates operate on RAM-resident state
Any asynchronous disk write makes a database in-memory
Disk stores only indexes, never data
The label depends only on using memory-mapped files

questions.explanation: An in-memory database is defined by keeping the data structures used for normal reads and updates in RAM, not by never touching disk. Logs and snapshots can provide restart recovery, backups, and replication without making disk the primary query path.

questions.question: Which of these in-memory data stores used a relational data model at the time of writing (2017)?

options.text: VoltDB, MemSQL, and Oracle TimesTen
RAMCloud, Redis, and Couchbase
Redis, Couchbase, and Oracle TimesTen
Memcached, RAMCloud, and VoltDB

questions.explanation: VoltDB, MemSQL and Oracle TimesTen were in-memory databases with a relational model, whose vendors claimed large performance gains from removing the overheads of on-disk data structures. RAMCloud is an open source in-memory key-value store with durability, Redis and Couchbase are non-relational stores that provide weak durability by writing to disk asynchronously, and Memcached is a key-value cache.

questions.question: What is the main reason in-memory databases can be faster than disk-based databases?

options.text: Not avoiding disk reads, which the OS cache can serve, but avoiding encoding in-memory structures for disk
Simply that RAM has far lower latency than disk, so every read is faster; no other factor contributes meaningfully
They skip durability entirely and never write a log or snapshot, so no time is spent on persistence of any kind
They use vectorized processing over compressed columns, which disk-based databases are unable to perform

questions.explanation: Counterintuitively, the speed of in-memory databases does not come mainly from not reading disk: a disk-based engine with enough memory may also never read from disk, because the operating system caches recently used disk blocks. The real gain is avoiding the overhead of encoding in-memory data structures in a form that can be written to disk. Many in-memory databases still write logs or snapshots for durability, and vectorized columnar processing is an analytics technique unrelated to being in-memory.

questions.question: Besides performance, what else do in-memory databases make possible?

options.text: Data models awkward on disk, as Redis does with queues and sets
Transactional guarantees stronger than any disk-based system offers
Replication being built in rather than bolted on afterwards
Schema-on-read flexibility that disk engines cannot provide

questions.explanation: Beyond speed, keeping everything in memory makes it practical to offer data models that are hard to implement with disk-based indexes. Redis, for example, offers a database-like interface to data structures such as priority queues and sets, and because all data is in memory its implementation is comparatively simple. Stronger transactional guarantees, built-in replication, and schema flexibility are not things that being in-memory specifically provides.

questions.question: Describe the anti-caching approach and the limitation it still has.

options.text: It evicts least-recently-used records to disk and reloads them on access, per record; indexes must still fit in memory
It compresses cold records in place inside memory instead of evicting them; the whole uncompressed dataset must still fit in memory
It replicates cold records to other machines and fetches them over the network; access patterns must be uniform across all keys
It is identical to operating-system swapping of memory pages, so it gives no advantage; and it removes the need for any index
