questions.explanation: Anti-caching evicts cold records from application-managed memory and reloads them when accessed, much like virtual memory at record rather than page granularity. The important limit remains: the index used to locate those records must still fit in RAM.

questions.question: Which emerging hardware technology could require further changes to storage engine design, and how settled was that expectation at the time of writing?

options.text: Non-volatile memory; changes are probably needed if it is widely adopted, but research is still new
Quantum storage; it will certainly force every storage engine to be redesigned within the next few years
Shingled magnetic recording; it has already forced every storage engine to be redesigned around it
Persistent GPU memory; it is considered irrelevant to storage engine design and is not worth watching

questions.explanation: Non-volatile memory (NVM) keeps its contents without power while being accessed like memory, which blurs the line between RAM and disk that current storage engines are built around. Further changes to engine design will probably be needed if NVM is widely adopted, but at the time of writing this was a new area of research worth watching, not a settled outcome.

questions.question: Where does the word 'transaction' come from, and what is the modern definition?

options.text: Business deals such as sales; now any group of reads and writes forming a logical unit
Double-entry bookkeeping in accounting; it now means a single write applied atomically
Telephone exchange switching terminology; it now means one request and its response
The ACID literature of the 1980s; it now means any operation running in full isolation

questions.explanation: In early business data processing, a write to the database usually corresponded to a commercial transaction: making a sale, placing an order with a supplier, or paying an employee's salary. As databases spread to data where no money changes hands, such as blog comments or game actions, the word stuck but its meaning widened: a transaction is now any group of reads and writes that form a logical unit. The word alone does not promise ACID guarantees, and it does not mean a single atomic write or a single request-response pair.

questions.question: Does a transaction have to be ACID, and what does transaction processing actually mean?

options.text: No; it just means letting clients make low-latency reads and writes, as opposed to periodic batch jobs
Yes; every transaction is ACID by definition, and transaction processing means running only ACID operations
Yes; transaction processing means only operations that move money, each of which must be fully ACID
No; transaction processing means periodic batch jobs that run once per day over accumulated data

questions.explanation: Transaction processing means serving low-latency reads and writes as requests arrive; it does not imply that every operation has full ACID guarantees. Batch processing instead runs bounded jobs periodically over accumulated data, such as a daily report.

questions.question: Describe the OLTP access pattern, and expand the acronym.

options.text: A few records fetched by key via an index; online transaction processing
Many records scanned and aggregated per query; online table processing
Bulk writes applied once per day in a window; offline transaction processing
Whole tables read into memory and joined; optimized lookup transaction processing

questions.explanation: Online transaction processing (OLTP) describes interactive applications that typically look up a small number of records by some key, using an index, and insert or update records based on user input. The name comes from business transactions, but the same pattern applies to blog comments, game actions or address books. Scanning and aggregating many records per query is the analytic (OLAP) pattern, and daily bulk jobs are batch processing.

questions.question: Which of these are characteristic of analytic (OLAP) access patterns? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Scan a huge number of records, read a few columns each, and compute aggregates
What was each store's total revenue in January? How many extra bananas sold during the promotion?
Which brand of baby food is most often bought together with brand X diapers?
What is the current balance of account 12345, as of the most recent posted entry?

questions.explanation: An analytic query usually scans a huge number of records, reads only a few columns of each, and returns aggregate statistics such as counts, sums or averages rather than raw data. Typical examples are total revenue per store in January, extra bananas sold during a promotion, or which baby food brand is most often bought with a given diaper brand. Such queries are usually written by business analysts for business intelligence. Looking up one account's current balance is a small keyed lookup, which is the OLTP pattern.

optionExplanations.a: Analytical queries commonly touch many rows but only selected columns, then return aggregates such as sums or counts. This pattern motivates columnar layouts and compression.
optionExplanations.b: Totals by store and promotional uplift require grouping and aggregating many sales events rather than fetching one current record. They are representative business-intelligence questions.
optionExplanations.c: Market-basket analysis correlates products across large collections of transactions to find co-purchase patterns. It is exploratory aggregation, not a point lookup.
optionExplanations.d: Fetching one account's latest balance is a selective, low-latency operational request. That access pattern is characteristic of OLTP rather than a warehouse scan.

questions.question: Expand OLAP, and how clear-cut is the OLTP/OLAP distinction?

options.text: Online analytic processing; the difference is not always clear-cut
Offline analytic processing; the distinction from OLTP is sharp and well defined
Optimized aggregate processing; the distinction is defined by data volume
Online aggregate protocol; the distinction is mainly a matter of vendor marketing

questions.explanation: OLAP means online analytical processing. The boundary with OLTP is a workload distinction rather than a strict product category: OLTP serves frequent small operational requests, while OLAP supports interactive exploration and aggregation over large datasets.

questions.question: Which dataset sizes are typical for OLTP and for OLAP?

options.text: Gigabytes to terabytes for OLTP; terabytes to petabytes for OLAP
Megabytes to gigabytes for OLTP; gigabytes to terabytes for OLAP
Terabytes to petabytes for OLTP; gigabytes to terabytes for OLAP
Gigabytes to terabytes for both OLTP and OLAP

questions.explanation: OLTP systems hold the latest state of operational data and typically range from gigabytes to terabytes. OLAP systems hold a history of events accumulated over time, often from many OLTP sources, so they typically range from terabytes to petabytes. Other typical contrasts: OLTP reads a few records by key and writes with low latency from user input, while OLAP aggregates over many records and is loaded by bulk import (ETL) or event streams.

questions.question: When did analytics move out of OLTP databases, and what was the separate database called?

options.text: Late 1980s and early 1990s, into a data warehouse
Late 1990s, into what was then called a data lake
The 1970s, into a decision support system
The 2000s, into what is now called a lakehouse

questions.explanation: During the late 1980s and early 1990s, organizations increasingly copied analytical data out of transaction-processing systems into separate data warehouses. The separation allowed each system to optimize for a different access pattern without analytical scans disrupting OLTP.

questions.question: State the two expectations placed on OLTP systems and the harm an ad hoc analytic query does.

options.text: High availability and low latency; big ad hoc scans slow concurrent transactions
Durability and consistency; ad hoc queries can corrupt data that transactions are writing
Scalability and low cost; ad hoc queries exhaust available disk space
Schema flexibility; ad hoc queries invalidate the existing schema

questions.explanation: OLTP systems are often critical to running the business, so they are expected to be highly available and to process transactions with low latency. Ad hoc analytic queries are often expensive and scan large parts of the dataset, so running them on an OLTP database can harm the performance of concurrently executing transactions. That resource contention is why administrators guard OLTP databases; analytic reads do not corrupt data or change the schema.

questions.question: Define a data warehouse and expand ETL, listing the stages of getting data in.

options.text: A read-only copy of OLTP data for analysts to query; Extract-Transform-Load
A write-optimized replica of the OLTP database; Extract-Transfer-Log
A cache holding the reports that analysts run most often; Evaluate-Transform-Load
A distributed filesystem holding raw files; Export-Translate-Load

questions.explanation: A data warehouse is a separate analytical repository populated from operational systems. ETL extracts data by dumps or streams, transforms and cleans it into an analysis-friendly schema, and loads it. Analysts can then run expensive queries without disrupting customer-facing transactions.

questions.question: Why are data warehouses almost unheard of in small companies? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: They probably don't have many different OLTP systems to integrate
Their data is small enough for a conventional SQL database or a spreadsheet
Warehouse software is not made available to smaller companies
Small companies do not run analytics of any kind

questions.explanation: Small organizations may have few source systems and can query them directly without a dedicated integration platform. Large organizations must reconcile many teams, formats, meanings, and ownership boundaries, making extraction, cleaning, governance, and loading substantial engineering work.

optionExplanations.a: A small company may have only one or a few operational systems, so there is little cross-system extraction and reconciliation to justify a separate warehouse. Direct queries can remain manageable.
optionExplanations.b: When data fits comfortably in a conventional database or spreadsheet, the organization can analyze it without specialized warehouse infrastructure. Scale has not yet forced a separate engine.
optionExplanations.c: Warehouse technology is available to organizations of many sizes, including managed services. Its rarity in small companies follows from need and complexity, not a vendor prohibition.
optionExplanations.d: Small companies still use reports, spreadsheets, and analytical queries. They may simply perform them on simpler systems rather than operating a dedicated warehouse.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of running analytics on a separate data warehouse rather than directly on OLTP systems, and what does it imply about indexes designed for OLTP?

options.text: The warehouse can be optimized for analytic access; OLTP-style indexes answer analytic queries poorly
The warehouse is cheaper to license; OLTP-style indexes answer analytic queries just as well as they answer lookups
The warehouse is more durable; OLTP-style indexes are needed mainly to protect analytic data against loss
The warehouse has a flexible schema; OLTP-style indexes become obsolete for transactional workloads too

questions.explanation: A separate warehouse can choose storage layouts, compression, execution strategies and indexes specifically for large analytical scans, without slowing the business-critical OLTP systems. Indexes built for OLTP, such as hash indexes, B-trees and LSM-trees, are designed to find a few records by key quickly; they remain the right tool for transactional workloads, but they are not very good at queries that scan and aggregate a large fraction of a table, which is what analytics mostly does.

questions.question: What data model do data warehouses most commonly use, and how do they compare with relational OLTP databases?

options.text: Relational, as SQL suits analytics; same SQL surface as OLTP but very different internals
Document-oriented, because analytics data arrives deeply nested from source systems
Graph-oriented, because warehouse dimensions are richly interconnected with each other
Key-value, because analytic queries almost always look rows up by their primary key

questions.explanation: Data warehouses are most commonly relational, because SQL is generally a good fit for analytic queries and many graphical analysis tools generate SQL, visualize results, and support drill-down and slicing and dicing. On the surface a warehouse and a relational OLTP database look similar because both offer a SQL interface, but their internals can be very different because they are optimized for very different query patterns. That is why, at the time of writing, many vendors focused on either transaction processing or analytics, but not both.

questions.question: Which statements describe the data warehouse market as it stood around 2017? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: SQL Server and SAP HANA supported both workloads, but increasingly as two engines behind one SQL interface
Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA and ParAccel were sold under expensive licences; Amazon Redshift was a hosted ParAccel
Open source SQL-on-Hadoop projects had proliferated: Hive, Spark SQL, Impala, Presto, Tajo and Drill
Every data warehouse product on the market was open source and free of any licence cost

questions.explanation: At the time, some databases such as Microsoft SQL Server and SAP HANA supported both transaction processing and warehousing, but increasingly as two separate storage and query engines behind a common SQL interface. Warehouse vendors such as Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA and ParAccel typically sold expensive commercial licences, and Amazon Redshift was a hosted version of ParAccel. A number of young open source SQL-on-Hadoop projects aimed to compete with them, some based on ideas from Google's Dremel. Commercial products were a major part of the market, so it was not all open source.

optionExplanations.a: SQL Server and SAP HANA offered transactional and analytical support in one product, but increasingly through distinct internal engines behind one SQL surface. A shared interface does not imply one identical storage path.
optionExplanations.b: The commercial warehouse market included costly products such as Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA and ParAccel, with Amazon Redshift based on hosted ParAccel technology. This is a historical snapshot of that market.
optionExplanations.c: Projects including Hive, Spark SQL, Impala, Presto, Tajo and Drill brought SQL analytics to the Hadoop ecosystem. They were young but aimed to compete with proprietary warehouse engines.
optionExplanations.d: Commercially licensed warehouses were a major part of the market, so it is false that every product was open source and free. Open SQL-on-Hadoop systems emerged as an alternative, not the only category.

questions.question: Contrast the variety of data models in transactional and analytic worlds, and give both names for the analytic style.

options.text: Far less diversity, being formulaic: star schema, or dimensional modeling
Analytics has more model diversity; the style is called normalized modeling
Both worlds use only relational models; the style is called cube modeling
Analytics uses graph models; the style is called network modeling

questions.explanation: Transactional systems use many models—relational, document, key-value, and graph—because application access patterns vary. Analytical warehouses converge more often on a formulaic relational style called dimensional modeling or a star schema, optimized for aggregation.

questions.question: What sits at the centre of a star schema, and what does one row mean?

options.text: A fact table such as fact_sales; each row is one event
A dimension table; each row represents one business entity
An aggregate table; each row holds one precomputed total
A date table; each row represents a single calendar day

questions.explanation: A fact table sits at the center, and each row records one event such as a sale line item. In a website-traffic warehouse, the corresponding fact might instead be a page view or click; dimensions describe the entities and context around that event.

questions.question: Why do fact tables get enormous, and at what scale?

options.text: Each event is stored individually, not pre-aggregated; big enterprises hold tens of petabytes
Facts are duplicated once per dimension they reference; even the largest hold a few terabytes
Facts are never deleted once written; only a single web company has reached even one petabyte
Facts inline every dimension attribute they need; typical warehouses hold tens of gigabytes

questions.explanation: Facts are usually captured as individual events, such as each customer's purchase of a product, because that allows maximum flexibility for later analysis; the price is that fact tables become extremely large. Big enterprises such as Apple, Walmart or eBay have had tens of petabytes of transaction history in their warehouses, most of it in fact tables. Fact rows reference dimensions by foreign key rather than duplicating or inlining their attributes, which is why dimension tables stay comparatively small.

questions.question: Which two kinds of columns normally appear in a fact table?

options.text: Attributes such as price and cost, and foreign keys to dimension tables
Precomputed aggregates, and pointers to rows in other fact tables
Only foreign keys, because all measures are stored in dimension tables
Free-text descriptions of products, stores and customers

questions.explanation: A fact row records an event. Numeric measures such as sale price and supplier cost support aggregation, while foreign keys connect it to descriptive dimensions. Those dimensions supply the who, what, where, when, how, and why needed for analysis.

questions.question: Why represent a date with a dimension table rather than only a raw date value?

options.text: Extra facts about each date, such as public holidays, can be stored and queried
Fact tables cannot contain date or timestamp columns, so dates must live elsewhere
Only a dimension table lets the fact table be sorted or partitioned by date
Raw date values cannot be converted between time zones, while a dimension table can

questions.explanation: In a star schema, even dates are often modeled as a dimension table. Each fact row refers to a date key, and the date dimension stores additional information about each date, such as whether it is a public holiday, so queries can, for example, compare sales on holidays with sales on other days. A raw date column carries only the date itself. Fact tables can contain dates, and sorting or time-zone handling do not require a dimension table.

questions.question: How does a snowflake schema differ from a star schema?

options.text: It normalizes dimensions further into subdimension tables that dimensions reference
It denormalizes all dimension attributes into one wide fact table with no joins
It splits the fact table into several smaller fact tables, one per dimension
It removes the central fact table and keeps only the dimension tables

questions.explanation: In a star schema, a central fact table references dimension tables, and drawn out it looks like a star. A snowflake schema further breaks dimensions into subdimensions; for example, the product dimension can reference separate brand and category tables instead of storing them as strings. Snowflake schemas are more normalized, but star schemas are often preferred because they are simpler for analysts to work with. Both keep the fact table at the centre.

questions.question: How wide are warehouse tables, and what fraction of a fact table row does a typical query actually need?

options.text: Often over 100 columns, sometimes several hundred; a typical query reads only 4 or 5
About ten columns in total, and a typical analytic query reads most of them
Several thousand columns, of which a typical query reads roughly half at a time
About a hundred columns, of which a typical query genuinely needs around eighty

questions.explanation: Fact tables in a typical warehouse often have over 100 columns and sometimes several hundred, and dimension tables can also be wide because they hold all metadata that might be useful for analysis, such as a store's services, square footage and opening date. Yet a typical warehouse query accesses only 4 or 5 columns at a time, and SELECT * is rarely needed. That mismatch between table width and the columns a query uses is what makes column-oriented storage pay off.

questions.question: In row-oriented storage, why does an index on fact_sales.date_key or fact_sales.product_sk still leave an analytic query that touches many rows slow?

options.text: Rows are stored whole, so it must load and parse every 100-plus-column row to use a few columns
The index is not kept sorted, so the engine must fall back to a full scan of the table for every query
An index cannot be combined with a GROUP BY clause, so the engine ignores it for grouped queries
The index covers only the dimension tables, never the fact table, so it cannot locate fact rows

questions.explanation: Row-oriented storage keeps all values of one row next to each other, as most OLTP databases (and document databases, per document) do. An index on date_key or product_sk tells the engine where the matching rows are, but the engine still has to load each of those rows, with all of its 100-plus attributes, from disk into memory, parse them, and filter them, even though the query needs only a few columns. The index solves locating rows, not the cost of reading wide rows; column-oriented storage addresses that cost.

questions.question: State the column-oriented idea in one sentence.

options.text: Store all values of each column together, so reads touch only those used
Store each row twice over, once in sorted order and once in insertion order
Keep every column resident in memory while the rows themselves stay on disk
Store only those columns that already carry a secondary index on them

questions.explanation: Column-oriented storage keeps each column in a separate file or region, so a query reads and parses only the fields it needs. Analytical queries often touch many rows but few columns, making this layout much cheaper than loading every field from each selected row.

questions.question: Does column storage require a relational model, and what does Parquet demonstrate?

options.text: No; it applies to nonrelational data too, as Parquet does for a document data model
Yes; it works only with relational models, and Parquet stores documents row by row
Yes; it requires a fixed relational schema, which Parquet enforces on every file
No; column storage is itself a data model, so Parquet replaces the relational model

questions.explanation: Column-oriented storage is a physical layout choice: store all the values of each column together instead of all the values of each row. It is easiest to picture with relational tables, but it applies equally to nonrelational data. Parquet, for example, is a columnar storage format that supports a document data model, based on Google's Dremel. The logical data model and the physical layout are independent choices.

questions.question: What invariant does column-oriented storage rely on to reassemble rows?

options.text: All column files keep rows in one order, so the kth entries form row k
Every column file is sorted independently according to its own values
Every column file must occupy exactly the same number of bytes on disk
Every column file carries its own copy of the table's primary key column

questions.explanation: In a column store each column is stored separately, so the only link between values of the same row is their position. Every column file must contain the rows in the same order; then the 23rd entry in each column file together forms the 23rd row of the table. Sorting each column independently would destroy that link, and column files need not be the same size on disk. The same positional correspondence is what lets bitmaps from different columns be combined with bitwise AND or OR.

questions.question: Why does column data compress well, and which technique suits data warehouses particularly?

options.text: The values within a column are often repetitive; bitmap encoding is particularly effective in warehouses
Column values are mostly unique per row; delta encoding is particularly effective in warehouses
Each column is stored sorted by its own values; dictionary encoding is particularly effective in warehouses
Column data is small in volume; plain gzip is particularly effective in warehouses

questions.explanation: Values within one column often repeat and share a type, which makes them highly compressible. Bitmap encoding is especially useful for low-cardinality warehouse columns: one bitmap per distinct value turns filters into fast bitwise operations while reducing bytes read.

questions.question: Define bitmap encoding precisely, and explain what is done when the bitmaps are sparse.

options.text: One bitmap per distinct value, one bit per row; sparse ones are run-length encoded
One bitmap per row with one bit per distinct value; sparse bitmaps are discarded
A hash of each value per row; sparse values fall back to plain strings
A sorted list of the distinct values; sparse columns are left unencoded

questions.explanation: Bitmap encoding turns a column with n distinct values into n bitmaps, one per distinct value, each with one bit per row; the bit is 1 if that row has the value and 0 otherwise. When n is small (a country column has about 200 values), the bitmaps can be stored with one bit per row. When n is large, most bitmaps are mostly zeros (sparse), so they are additionally run-length encoded. For example, a retailer with a billion sales rows and 100,000 distinct products would need 100,000 × 10^9 = 10^14 bits, about 12.5 TB, if the bitmaps were stored raw; run-length encoding makes this compact.

questions.question: In a column store with bitmap-encoded columns, one query filters product_sk IN (30, 68, 69); another filters product_sk = 31 AND store_sk = 3. What bitwise operations evaluate these filters?

options.text: OR the three bitmaps, then AND the two; valid because all column files share one row order
An AND of three bitmaps then an OR of two; validity comes from each column being sorted
Both become XOR operations over the bitmaps; validity comes from the stored checksums
Bitmap columns cannot be combined at all, so each predicate is evaluated as a separate scan

questions.explanation: For the IN filter, the engine loads the three bitmaps for product_sk = 30, 68 and 69 and computes their bitwise OR, which marks every row matching any of the values. For the AND filter, it loads the bitmap for product_sk = 31 and the bitmap for store_sk = 3 and computes their bitwise AND. Combining bitmaps from different columns works because every column stores rows in the same order, so the kth bit in each bitmap refers to the same row. Sorting and checksums are not what make this valid.

questions.question: Cassandra and HBase use Bigtable-style column families. Why is it misleading to call them column-oriented?

options.text: Each column family stores a row's columns together with the row key, uncompressed by column, so storage is mostly row-oriented
They do store each column in its own separate file, but they cannot compress those column files, so they are only partly columnar
Column families are really relational tables, so their data model is relational and the storage layout is irrelevant
They store their data in B-trees rather than LSM-trees, and B-trees cannot hold column-oriented data at all

questions.explanation: Cassandra and HBase organize data into column families, but within a family they store a row key together with that row's columns. They therefore remain mostly row-oriented and do not use the per-column compression and scan layout associated with analytical column stores.

questions.question: Disk-to-memory bandwidth is a big bottleneck but not the only one. Which others do developers of analytical databases worry about? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Using the bandwidth from main memory into the CPU cache efficiently
Avoiding branch mispredictions and bubbles in the CPU pipeline
Making use of single-instruction-multi-data instructions in modern CPUs
Reducing the number of network round-trips to the storage layer

questions.explanation: Once disk reads are reduced, CPU efficiency matters: engines try to move data through memory caches efficiently, avoid unpredictable branches that stall pipelines, and process many values per instruction with SIMD. Vectorized execution targets all three.

optionExplanations.a: After disk I/O falls, moving column batches efficiently from main memory into CPU caches becomes a bottleneck. Cache-friendly contiguous processing reduces wasted memory bandwidth.
optionExplanations.b: Unpredictable branches can flush or stall CPU pipelines, creating bubbles even when data is already in memory. Vectorized operators reduce branch-heavy per-row control flow.
optionExplanations.c: SIMD instructions apply one operation to several values at once, increasing arithmetic throughput for scans and aggregates. Columnar batches place same-type values in a suitable layout.
optionExplanations.d: Network round trips can matter in a distributed warehouse, but they are not a CPU-side bottleneck of scanning data inside one node. Memory bandwidth, branch prediction and SIMD use are what vectorized execution targets.

questions.question: Define vectorized processing and explain how columnar layout helps the CPU.

options.text: Loop over an L1-resident chunk, operating on the compressed form directly
Use GPUs rather than CPUs for the aggregation work, since GPUs have wider registers
Decompress each column block first, then process the resulting rows one at a time
Spread every query across many machines so each handles a slice of the columns

questions.explanation: Vectorized processing means operating on a chunk of column values at a time in a tight loop, rather than processing one record at a time through many function calls and conditions. A query engine can take a chunk of compressed column data that fits comfortably in the CPU's L1 cache and iterate through it with no function calls, which a CPU executes much faster. Column compression lets more rows fit in the same cache, and operators such as bitwise AND and OR can work directly on the compressed chunks. GPUs and distributing across machines are separate techniques.

questions.question: In a column-oriented store, which row order is easiest to maintain, and what does deliberately imposing a sort order buy you?

options.text: Insertion order, since inserting just appends; an imposed order indexes it
Sorted order is easiest; imposing insertion order is what enables compression
Random order is easiest; imposing an order is what enables replication
Reverse insertion order is easiest; imposing an order enables deletion

questions.explanation: Rows in a column store can be stored in any order, and the easiest is insertion order, because adding a row then just means appending a value to each column file. Alternatively, the store can impose a sort order on the rows, as SSTables do with keys, and use that order as an indexing mechanism: for example, a query on a date range can read only the rows in that range. Sorting also helps compression, but it is not required for replication or deletion.

questions.question: In a column-oriented store, why can't each column be sorted independently of the others?

options.text: Row reconstruction needs the kth item of each column to be the same row
Because sorting each column separately is computationally too expensive
Because compression algorithms require one global ordering
Because the query optimizer assumes insertion order throughout

questions.explanation: A column store reconstructs a row by taking the kth item from every column, so the kth items of all columns must belong to the same row. Sorting each column by its own values would scramble those positions and make it impossible to know which values belong together. So the data is sorted an entire row at a time, using chosen sort-key columns, even though it is stored by column. The constraint is about correctness, not the cost of sorting.

questions.question: Who normally chooses a column store's physical sort order?

options.text: An administrator, based on common query patterns
The optimizer permanently rewrites physical order for every query
The engine chooses only from column cardinality
Each application query supplies a different physical sort order

questions.explanation: The database administrator chooses the sort columns ahead of time, using knowledge of the common queries; the optimizer does not rewrite physical order per query. A leading date_key lets range queries skip old data; a second product_sk groups rows for the same product within each date, improving filters and aggregations that use both.

questions.question: In a column store, why does sorting rows help compression, and how does the benefit change for the second, third and later sort keys?

options.text: Few distinct values give long runs; later sort keys are jumbled
Sorting helps every column equally, since each column file is compressed independently
Sorting actively hurts compression, which is why insertion order is usually preferred
Sorting only improves the compression of numeric columns, not string-valued ones

questions.explanation: If the first sort column has few distinct values, sorting places equal values next to each other in long runs, which simple run-length encoding can compress to a few kilobytes even for billions of rows. The second sort key is ordered only within each run of the first, so its runs are shorter, and the third even more so; columns far down the sort priority are in essentially random order and compress less well. Having the first few columns sorted is still a win overall. Sorting helps string and numeric columns alike.

questions.question: Whose idea was storing several different sort orders, and what makes it almost free?

options.text: C-Store, adopted by Vertica; replication already duplicates the data
Bigtable, adopted by HBase; compression makes the extra copies cheap
Dremel, adopted by Parquet; the columnar layout makes copies free
Hive; it is free simply because storage has become inexpensive

questions.explanation: Different queries benefit from different sort orders, and data needs replicating anyway so you don't lose it when a machine fails — so store that redundant data sorted differently and use whichever version fits the query. The redundancy you already pay for is repurposed for performance. The idea was introduced in the C-Store research system and adopted in the commercial data warehouse Vertica.

questions.question: In a column store, keeping several copies of the data, each sorted in a different order, resembles which row-store feature, and where does the resemblance break down?

options.text: Secondary indexes; but a column store has no pointers, so each sort order is a full copy
Materialized views; but a view is virtual rather than an actual copy stored on disk
Table partitioning; but partitions are disjoint subsets of rows rather than overlapping full copies
Replication; but replicas are byte-identical to one another rather than reordered

questions.explanation: Storing the same data in several sort orders lets each query use the copy whose order best fits it, which is a bit like a row-oriented store having several secondary indexes. The difference is that a row store keeps every row in one place (a heap file or clustered index) and its secondary indexes hold only pointers to matching rows. A column store normally has no pointers to data elsewhere, only columns of values, so each sort order is a complete copy of the data rather than a lightweight index. Materialized views are actual copies, partitions do split rows into disjoint sets, and replicas are often identical, but none of those is the analogy being drawn.

questions.question: In a column store that compresses and sorts its column files, why are writes difficult? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Update-in-place, as B-trees do, is not possible with compressed columns
Inserting mid-table would mean rewriting every column file consistently
Column files cannot be appended to under any circumstances
Each write requires a distributed transaction across the column files

questions.explanation: Compression and sort order make reads faster but make writes harder. A compressed column cannot be updated in place the way a B-tree overwrites a page, because one value is packed together with its neighbours. And because rows are identified by their position within each column, inserting a row in the middle of a sorted table would mean rewriting every column file consistently. Appending new rows is still possible, and no distributed transaction is inherently required; column stores usually buffer writes and merge them in bulk.

optionExplanations.a: Compressed column files encode many values together, so overwriting one field in place can invalidate compression and positional structure. The engine instead creates new batches and merges them later.
optionExplanations.b: A row's position must correspond across every column; inserting into the middle of one file shifts that alignment. Preserving it would require coordinated rewrites of all affected column files.
optionExplanations.c: Column stores can append new batches or immutable files and later merge them, as Vertica does with an in-memory write area. The restriction is on arbitrary in-place insertion, not all appends.
optionExplanations.d: A write path may coordinate several columns, but it does not inherently require a distributed transaction for each row. Buffering and bulk merging solve the layout problem without that universal requirement.

questions.question: How can a column store avoid expensive row-by-row updates to compressed files?

options.text: Buffer writes in memory, as an LSM-tree does, and periodically merge them into new column files in bulk
Update each compressed column file in place row by row, using a B-tree over row positions to find each value
Append each new row to a separate row-oriented heap file that analytic queries never read
Decompress the entire table into memory on every write and recompress all column files afterwards

questions.explanation: Updating compressed column files row by row is expensive. Vertica accumulates writes in an in-memory store and periodically merges batches into new column files, applying the same buffered-write principle as an LSM-tree.

questions.question: A column store buffers recent writes in memory and merges them into column files later. What must queries do, and what does an analyst see?

options.text: Examine disk columns and memory writes together, hidden by the optimizer
Read only the on-disk columns, leaving recent writes invisible until the next merge
Be re-run by hand once each background merge into the column files has completed
Read the in-memory store for new data only when given an explicit query flag

questions.explanation: Recent writes live in the in-memory store until the next merge, so queries must read both the column files on disk and the recent writes in memory and combine the results. The query optimizer hides this split from the user: from an analyst's point of view, inserts, updates and deletes are reflected in subsequent queries immediately, without waiting for a merge or using special flags.

questions.question: How universal is column-oriented storage among data warehouses, and what speed advantage does it offer?

options.text: Not every warehouse is columnar, but columnar storage can be significantly faster for ad hoc analytics
Every warehouse is a column store, because row-oriented layouts cannot execute analytic SQL queries at all
Few warehouses are columnar, because columnar storage is consistently slower for ad hoc analytic queries
Columnar storage is used only for materialized views, never for the raw fact tables of a warehouse

questions.explanation: Column orientation is common but not universal among warehouses. For ad hoc analytics it can be much faster because a query reads only the referenced columns, those columns compress well, and vectorized execution processes them efficiently; row-oriented warehouses remain viable for other workloads.

questions.question: In a data warehouse, why can it be worth caching the results of aggregates such as COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN or MAX?

options.text: Many queries reuse the same aggregates, so recomputing them from the raw data each time is wasteful
Aggregates cannot be computed on column-oriented storage, so they must be precomputed elsewhere
Caching aggregates removes any need to keep the raw fact data in the warehouse
Aggregate functions give different results on each run, so caching keeps answers consistent

questions.explanation: Warehouse queries often use aggregate functions over large numbers of rows. If the same aggregates are used by many different queries, crunching through the raw data each time repeats the same work, so it can pay to cache the most frequently used counts or sums, for example as a materialized view or data cube. Raw data is still kept for flexibility, aggregates can be computed on any storage layout, and they are deterministic.

questions.question: Define materialized view versus virtual view, and describe what the SQL engine does when you read from each.

options.text: Virtual views expand on the fly; materialized views are a copy on disk
Materialized views are a shortcut for writing queries; virtual views are copies on disk
Both are copies written to disk, differing only in how often each is refreshed
Both are expanded on the fly at query time, differing only in whether results get cached

questions.explanation: Both are table-like objects defined by a query. A virtual view is just a shortcut for writing queries: when you read from it, the SQL engine expands it into the underlying query on the fly and runs that. A materialized view is an actual copy of the query results written to disk, so reading it does not rerun the query, but it must be updated when the underlying data changes.

questions.question: Why must materialized views be maintained, and where do they belong?

options.text: They are denormalized copies, so writes cost more — rarely worth it in OLTP
They need no maintenance at all, since they are recomputed from scratch on every read
They belong in OLTP databases, where writes are cheap and reads are latency-critical
They must be refreshed by hand by whichever analyst originally created the view

questions.explanation: A materialized view is a denormalized copy of query results, so it must be updated whenever the underlying data changes. The database can do this automatically, but those updates make writes more expensive, which is why materialized views are not often used in OLTP databases. In read-heavy data warehouses they make more sense, though whether they actually improve read performance depends on the individual case.

questions.question: Give both names for the special case of a materialized view, and describe what aggregating along an axis yields.

options.text: Data cube or OLAP cube; aggregating along an axis gives one fewer dimension
Star cube or fact cube; aggregating along an axis adds a further dimension
Snowflake cube or dimension cube; aggregating along an axis returns the raw facts
Hypercube or pivot cube; aggregating along an axis yields a single scalar

questions.explanation: A data cube, also called an OLAP cube, precomputes aggregates for combinations of dimensions. Aggregating along one axis removes that dimension from the grouping—for example, summing across dates yields sales by product regardless of date.

questions.question: What is the main flexibility cost of a precomputed data cube?

options.text: It cannot filter on attributes that were not selected as dimensions
It must be recomputed for every query, so it is slower than raw scans
It can aggregate only with SUM, never with COUNT or AVG
It can answer questions about only one dimension at a time

questions.explanation: A cube trades flexibility for lookup speed by fixing dimensions and aggregates in advance. It can answer total sales per store quickly, but not an unplanned predicate such as items priced above $100 if price was not a cube dimension. Keeping raw facts preserves the ability to ask new questions.

questions.question: Storage engines split in two by workload. Which bottleneck belongs to which?

options.text: OLTP: small key lookups bound by seek time. Analytics: scans bound by bandwidth
OLTP is bound by disk bandwidth, whereas analytics is bound by disk seek time
Both OLTP and analytics turn out to be bound by disk seek time on modern hardware
Both OLTP and analytics are bound by available CPU rather than by the disk at all

questions.explanation: OLTP systems are user-facing and handle a huge volume of requests, each touching a small number of records found by key through an index, so disk seek time is often the bottleneck. Analytic systems handle far fewer queries, but each one scans many millions of records, so disk bandwidth rather than seek time is often the bottleneck, and column-oriented storage is an increasingly popular answer. CPU efficiency also matters in analytics, but it does not replace these disk bottlenecks.

questions.question: What is the defining difference between log-structured and update-in-place storage?

options.text: Log-structured engines only append and delete whole files; update-in-place ones overwrite fixed-size pages
Log-structured engines are row stores and update-in-place engines are column stores, matching OLTP and OLAP
Log-structured engines keep all data in memory, while update-in-place engines keep all data on disk
Log-structured engines use only hash indexes, while update-in-place engines use only sorted indexes

questions.explanation: The deep distinction is immutability versus overwriting. Log-structured engines append and later replace whole immutable files through compaction; B-tree engines modify fixed-size pages in place, supported by write-ahead logging and concurrency control.

questions.question: What single idea do log-structured engines contribute, and why does it matter for hardware?

options.text: Turning random writes into sequential ones, raising write throughput on hard drives and SSDs
Eliminating secondary indexes altogether, which greatly reduces memory pressure and write work
Compressing all stored data, which reduces the disk capacity a dataset requires
Avoiding the write-ahead log entirely, which halves the engine's write amplification

questions.explanation: Log-structured engines buffer and batch random logical updates into sequential file writes. Sequential access raises throughput on hard drives and remains useful on SSDs by reducing write amplification and improving I/O locality, even though SSD controllers already remap physical writes.

questions.question: Why are row-lookup indexes often less central—not irrelevant—for large analytical scans?

options.text: Large scans benefit more from reading fewer compressed bytes
Analytical queries almost always look up one primary key
Indexes cannot be built on fact tables
Materialized views eliminate every use for indexes

questions.explanation: Indexes still help selective analytical predicates, but many warehouse queries touch a large fraction of a table. In that case the dominant goal shifts from finding individual rows to scanning fewer columns and fewer compressed bytes efficiently.

questions.question: What can a developer who understands storage engine internals, but has never built one, realistically do with that knowledge?

options.text: Choose an engine and reason about its tuning knobs, but not tune one expertly
Implement a production-grade storage engine, with no remaining gaps in skill
Tune any engine to expert level, though OLAP internals stay out of reach
Predict exact query latency from first principles, without any benchmarking

questions.explanation: A rough mental model of what a storage engine does under the hood lets a developer choose an engine suited to the application's workload and imagine what effect raising or lowering a tuning parameter may have, and it gives enough vocabulary to make sense of a database's documentation. It does not make someone an expert tuner of any particular engine, a builder of production storage engines, or able to predict latency without benchmarking.
